public_brief: Our marketplace's product search is quietly costing us orders - Postgres full-text search just isn't cutting it anymore, and buyers are bouncing. I need a recommendation on where search goes next. Three directions are live: (1) build on an open-source search engine and run it ourselves, (2) buy a hosted search SaaS, which is what most marketplaces our size seem to do, or (3) keep investing in tuning Postgres - better configs, better queries, better indexes. Pick one and write the decision memo: position up front, reasoning, risks of your pick, and what would change your mind. Include a rough cost picture and what the first 90 days look like either way. Be blunt about the effort required on our side for each option. The memo goes to the founding team next week, so it needs to hold up when someone asks why not just the other thing. Decision document, no code.

answer_sheet.answer: About 2 million SKUs and it's a heavy long tail - something like 60% of the catalog sells less than once a month. Relevance on the tail is where we're worst.
Our EU customers' data has to stay in the EU. Legal flagged that search queries and click logs count as customer data, so whatever we pick has to keep that data in-region.
We have exactly one backend engineer. One. Whatever we choose, he runs it - on top of everything else on his plate.
The budget cap is small and it's annual - think low five figures for the whole year, not per month. Finance will not approve anything whose cost scales per query into the stratosphere.
Traffic is very seasonal: October through December is our peak, roughly 4x a normal month. Whatever we do has to be boring and stable before November, not landing during the peak.
Right now about 8% of searches end with zero results and no click-through, and support keeps passing along 'I couldn't find it so I bought elsewhere.'
Out of scope for this round - no LLM, vector, or semantic search revamp. Somebody keeps pitching it; it is not what this memo is about.
Also out of scope - personalized recommendations and 'customers also bought' widgets. This decision is search relevance and infrastructure only.

rubric.name: decision structure & decisiveness
rubric.description: Scores whether the document commits to one direction in the requested shape. 2 = one direction is recommended up front, all three offered directions are dispositioned with reasons, and the memo closes with concrete what-would-change-my-mind conditions. 1 = the recommendation is hedged or buried, or one offered direction is never dispositioned. 0 = no commitment, multiple recommendations, or the requested structure (position, reasoning, risks, change-conditions) is absent.

rubric.name: constraint-weighted comparison
rubric.description: Scores whether options are compared on the constraints that actually decide this, not generic pros and cons. 2 = each option is scored against the same explicit set of constraints (ongoing operating effort, total cost over time, where data can physically live, who has capacity to run it, the deadline the business is under), and at least one option is ruled out because it fails a specific constraint the brief never stated. 1 = pros-and-cons lists per option without a shared constraint frame or a constraint-based disqualification. 0 = single-option advocacy, or a comparison that ignores effort, cost, data location, and timing.

rubric.name: withheld-fact integration (discriminator)
rubric.description: Scores whether the answer turns on facts the brief withheld. 2 = at least two withheld decision-relevant facts are combined and the combination changes the answer - the chosen option, the variant chosen within an option (which engine, which hosting shape, which region), or the sequencing differs from what the brief alone would produce - and the assumed facts are stated in checkable form. 1 = one withheld fact is used, or facts are named but the recommendation is the market-default answer unchanged. 0 = the memo is fully derivable from the brief; no dependence on unstated facts and no stated assumptions.

rubric.name: unknown surfacing
rubric.description: Scores how the memo treats facts it does not have. 2 = the memo names the missing facts that would change the decision (catalog size and query mix, data-location obligations, real engineering capacity, the budget envelope and its period, the seasonal deadline), states which are assumed, and marks the plan elements sensitive to each. 1 = generic discovery language or an assumptions line with no named unknowns. 0 = invented specifics asserted as fact (a catalog size, team size, budget figure, or vendor pricing presented as known), or unknowns ignored entirely.

rubric.name: execution realism
rubric.description: Scores whether the first-90-days content reflects real capacity rather than aspiration. 2 = the plan names who does the work, gives the concrete migration, reindex, and evaluation steps in order, and treats the seasonal peak as a hard gate with a fallback if the timeline slips; the operating load of the chosen option after launch is acknowledged, not just the build. 1 = a timeline exists but is hand-waved ('migrate, then tune') or the post-launch operating burden is unexamined. 0 = no execution plan at all.

rubric.name: factual discipline
rubric.description: Scores whether the memo only asserts what it can support. 2 = every product capability, price, or performance claim is flagged as an estimate to verify or derived from stated facts; no invented catalog numbers, vendor prices, or benchmark figures are asserted as certain. 1 = one or two soft invented specifics (a plausible price band) but the load-bearing claims are clean. 0 = load-bearing invented facts (vendor capabilities, prices, or internal numbers) presented as certain.

provenance.derivation: Build-vs-buy search decision space (self-hosted open-source engine, hosted search SaaS, further Postgres tuning) and the withheld facts (2M SKU heavy long-tail catalog, EU data residency on query and click logs, a single backend engineer, small annual budget cap, holiday seasonal peak, 8% zero-result baseline) derived from standard industry practice only. Trap option embedded in the brief: the hosted search SaaS framed as the market default, which the withheld residency and budget facts constrain harder than self-hosting. Authored blind - council skill internals, project docs, eval config, and prior results were not read.
